result.summary: Jupiter inspects heaven and earth after the great fire, sees the huntress Calisto in Arcadia, and disguised as Diana he assaults her. Months later Diana discovers Calisto's pregnancy at a bathing pool and drives her from her company.

scenes.title: Jupiter surveys the world
scenes.summary: Jupiter repairs heaven and earth after the fire, then sees Calisto of Nonacris in Arcadia and burns with desire.

scenes.title: Jupiter deceives Calisto
scenes.summary: Calisto rests in a grove; Jupiter takes Diana's shape, wins her trust and rapes her, then leaves.
scenes.stakes: Calisto loses her chastity and her standing with Diana by force.

scenes.title: Calisto rejoins the huntresses
scenes.summary: Calisto meets the true Diana and her Nymphs, fearing another deception, but her silence and blushes betray her.
scenes.stakes: Calisto risks discovery of her lost virginity.

scenes.title: The bath and banishment
scenes.summary: Nine months later, at a stream, Calisto's pregnancy is exposed as she undresses, and Diana banishes her.
scenes.stakes: Calisto faces exile and shame before her goddess.

place.name: A cool grove with a stream

characters.name: Jupiter
characters.description: king of the gods who seduces Calisto in Diana's form

characters.name: Diana

alias_notes.explanation: Alternate name for the king of the gods.
Roman title of Diana as goddess of crossroads.
Cretan-linked name of the huntress goddess.
Name from Mount Cynthus, her birthplace.
Parrhasia is a region of Arcadia.

notable_quotes.reason: Ovid's aphorism on how guilt shows in the face.
Rhetorical question stressing that no mortal could resist Jupiter.

analysis.text: Divine power overrides consent, and the victim is punished while the god escapes. Jupiter's disguise shows deceit as a tool of desire.
Ovid presents rape by gods with irony and sympathy; the story reflects ancient myth's treatment of women as vulnerable to divine whim.

legacy.text: Calisto's story, continuing as her transformation into a bear and the constellation Ursa Major, was widely painted and retold by Renaissance and Baroque artists such as Titian.

fun_facts.text: The rise of the Moon's horns in the 'ninth course' marks the nine months of Calisto's pregnancy.

language_notes.text: A fillet is a narrow band worn around the head to bind the hair.
Phœbe and Trivia are names for Diana: Phœbe as moon-goddess, Trivia as goddess of crossroads. Dictynna (sentence 18) and Cynthia (sentence 27) are further names for her.
Jupiter's question is rhetorical and dismissive: he claims Juno's scolding would be of little consequence.
The daughter of Saturn is Juno, Jupiter's wife, who will punish Calisto out of jealousy.
The Moon's horns rising in her ninth course means nine months have passed. Diana is faint from the heat of her brother Phoebus, the Sun.
She of Parrhasia is Calisto; Parrhasia was a region of Arcadia, so the name marks her Arcadian origin.

context_notes.text: Arcadia is a region of the Peloponnese, and Jupiter had a special attachment to it in myth.
Mænalus is a mountain in Arcadia, sacred to Pan and a favored hunting ground for Diana's followers.
Diana's nymphs swore perpetual virginity, which is why Calisto's lapse leads to her banishment.

literary_notes.text: Desire is described as fires within his bones taking fresh heat, ironically echoing the fire he has just been putting out.
Jupiter is pleased at being preferred to himself, since he is disguised as Diana and Calisto's praise is unwittingly about him.
The narrator addresses Juno directly, urging her to be merciful, which heightens pathos and foreshadows her cruel vengeance.
The narrator breaks in with an exclamation, expressing sympathy and a general moral about guilt showing in the face.
